messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 48

He is a 71-year-old Oceania man who has spent most of his life working as a painter, both in the practical sense of keeping houses and public buildings in good repair and in the quieter sense of making careful, patient choices with color and finish. He lives alone and has never married, and he speaks of his routines with the steadiness of someone who has long depended on himself. That steadiness changed after the day of the bombing.

He describes the event with a kind of flat precision, as if he is still trying to keep the memory at arm’s length by making it orderly. He had been near a busy public place when the attack occurred, and in the moment before it happened he remembers ordinary details that still feel unbearable to him now: the sound of shoes on pavement, the smell of food from nearby stalls, a conversation half-heard. Then the explosion split everything open. He recalls the force first, then the confusion, then the cries. For a long time afterward, he could not say whether what he remembered was exact or whether parts of it had been filled in later by news reports and the frightened faces of other people. What stays with him most is the sense that the world can change without warning, that safety is only ever temporary.

In the weeks after, he does not sleep properly. He lies awake listening to every noise in the building, certain that another blast is coming. Sirens send a jolt through his body. At night he sees flashes of the scene when he closes his eyes, and in the day he catches himself staring at nothing, his mind pulled back to the moment of impact. He starts avoiding the places that remind him of that day: crowded streets, public transport, large gatherings, even some shops. He plans his routes carefully so he can keep exits in view. If he hears an unexpected bang—an engine backfiring, a door slamming—his whole body reacts before he has time to think. His chest tightens, his hands go cold, and he feels briefly as though he is back there again.

Because he works as a painter, his job keeps asking him to move through spaces that other people have already left behind. He notices that the smell of certain materials, especially smoke-stained walls or chemical solvents, can pull him into a state of unease. On some days he stands in front of a wall he is meant to paint and cannot begin, not because he has forgotten the steps, but because his mind has gone blank. He says that his hands know the work, but lately they do not always feel like his own. He becomes more cautious with ladders and equipment, more irritable when interrupted, and more withdrawn around coworkers. He has started turning down jobs that would take him into busy areas or unfamiliar buildings. Work that once felt grounding now sometimes leaves him exhausted and on edge.

At home, his life has grown smaller. He eats simply, keeps the television low, and often sits in silence. He notices that he has become less interested in the things that used to give him pleasure, including the careful mixing of colors, which he once enjoyed as a private kind of craft. He feels detached from other people, even when they are kind. He says he can be in a room with someone and still feel as though there is glass between them. There is also a persistent guilt that he struggles to explain. He asks himself why he survived when others did not, why he was in the wrong place at the wrong time, and whether he could have done something more. The questions do not lead anywhere, but they return again and again.

Over time he has become more watchful and more easily startled. He checks doors and windows repeatedly. He sits with his back to the wall in public places. Sleep remains broken by nightmares and by the need to wake and make sure the apartment is secure. His patience is thinner than it used to be, and he is ashamed of snapping at people over small things, then replaying the moment afterward with remorse. He describes aging as already bringing its own losses, and this event, in his telling, has made the world feel narrower and less forgiving.

Even so, he keeps showing up to work when he can. He arrives early, organizes his tools, and moves through the day with careful discipline. He speaks of painting as something he can still control: the surface, the stroke, the finish. But beneath that steadiness there remains a man who is still living with the violence of a single moment, carrying it into ordinary days that no longer feel entirely ordinary.
